source: Mednick (1962) The associative basis of the creative process
finding: Founding theory. Creativity is the forming of new combinations from remote associative elements. Creative people have flat associative hierarchies (many, broader links to a cue). Less creative people have steep hierarchies (few, common links). The Remote Associates Test (RAT) was built to measure this. Known here only through the descriptions in Kenett 2014 and Benedek and Neubauer 2013.
numbers: No numbers read from the original.
limits: Original not opened this session. Theory was verbal, with no formal network model and no direct test of the gradient.
agent_relevance: Gives the hypothesis behind O7 and S3 open mode: reach for remote seed concepts, not just the dominant associate.

source: Kenett, Anaki and Faust (2014) Investigating the structure of semantic networks in low and high creative persons
finding: First network-science test of Mednick. Group free-association networks of high-creative people (HSC) have shorter average paths and are less broken into sub-parts than those of low-creative people (LSC). The LSC network is more rigid and spread out.
numbers: 144 recruited, 139 analysed (47 men, 92 women, mean age 23). Free-association subsample: 33 LSC and 33 HSC (70 completed, 4 removed). 96 cue words in 24 categories, 1 minute per cue. Groups = lower and upper tertile of a decision tree on RAT, TACT creativity test and metaphor tasks. RAT 7.0 vs 13.2. Table 3: ASPL 4.6 (LSC) vs 3.93 (HSC); diameter 12 vs 8; modularity Q 0.62 vs 0.58; small-world S 6.86 vs 7.76; clustering CC 0.67 vs 0.66 (no difference); mean degree equal 5.88. All differ from random networks, p<0.001.
quote: the network of persons with low creative ability is more rigid, compared to the network of persons with high creative ability
limits: One network per group, so no per-person statistics and no test of the group difference beyond bootstrap on half of nodes (ASPL 3.19 vs 3.16, so the gap shrinks a lot). Modularity gap small and may reflect network size. Only 96 cues. Group sizes small. The text and Table 4 disagree on which group has larger S in the bootstrap. Accuracy effect on metaphors had p<0.08 but was called significant.
agent_relevance: The 'small effect, 139 people' claim in our row. A group-level, small-sample result. Treat as a hypothesis for seed-distance control in O7, not as a tuned parameter.

source: Kenett, Anaki and Faust (2014) same paper: fluency and node-impact controls
finding: HSC produced more unique responses per cue, which is a confound for network differences. When only the first 10 responses were used, the LSC network was still less connected and more spread out, but modularity reversed (lower for LSC).
numbers: Unique responses per word: ANOVA F(1,191)=310.9, p<0.001, eta2=0.614; HSC higher for 60% of words (BH-corrected p<0.01). Node impact Mann-Whitney U(192)=3523, z=-2.818, p<0.005; LSC 56% negative-impact nodes, HSC 65% positive-impact nodes. Creativity correlations are weak: RAT with TACT fluency r(137)=0.22; RAT with novel-metaphor RT r=-0.26; TACT quality with metaphor accuracy r=0.18.
limits: Fluency and structure are tangled: more responses can make a network denser by itself. The authors normalised only partly.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'more connected' may just mean 'more output'. For the agent, count of candidates and distance of candidates must be tracked separately.

source: Benedek and Neubauer (2013) Revisiting Mednick's model on creativity-related differences in associative hierarchies
finding: Direct test of Mednick's flat-versus-steep gradient. High and low creative people did NOT differ in associative hierarchies. High creative people were more fluent and gave more uncommon answers. The uncommonness gap mostly vanished when fluency was controlled.
numbers: N about 100 (df=98), continuous free association, 60 s per cue, groups from divergent thinking plus self-report. Strength of top-10 associates: ranking F(9,882)=83.33, eta2p=.46 (69.5% down to 21.7%); ranking x group F=0.98 ns; group F(1,98)=0.23 ns; slope difference b=-.052, t(98)=-0.28 ns. Fluency 16 vs 13 responses per minute, F(1,98)=40.73, eta2p=.29. Uncommonness F(1,98)=21.15, eta2p=.18; with fluency as covariate F(1,97)=3.32, p=.07, eta2p=.03. First 12 responses: group F(1,94)=7.19, p<.01, eta2p=.07.
quote: creativity may not be related to a special organization of associative memory, but rather to a more effective way of accessing its contents
limits: Single-word cues only, everyday (little-c) creativity, rare responses hard to measure because their strength is near zero. Does not test network path length.
agent_relevance: Key competing account: the difference is retrieval control and fluency, not a different memory. Supports G1-style control by code (keep generating, push later items) over trying to reshape the model's distribution.

source: Kenett, Levy, Kenett and Stanley (2018) Flexibility of thought in high creative individuals represented by percolation analysis (PNAS)
finding: Re-analysis of the same 2014 free-association data with percolation. Removing weak links breaks the low-creative network apart sooner than the high-creative one. This is the 'flexibility' claim.
numbers: 33 per group (66 total of 140 recruited), 96 cues. At threshold 0.1 LSC splits into 3 components, HSC stays whole. Percolation integral LSC 14.76 vs HSC 15.64 (about 6% higher). Noise test, 500 runs each: p<0.001 at SD 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01. Shuffled-link control reverses it: LSC 21.45 vs HSC 20.55, t(998)=19.25. Interlinks between components HSC 0.04 vs LSC 0.03 (U=5,226,777, p<0.001); intralinks equal (0.15 vs 0.15). 21 of 28 matched interlinks stronger in HSC. Component overlap about 87%.
limits: Same data and same 33 per group as the 2014 paper, so not an independent replication. Creativity treated as two groups. Link counts inconsistent (about 4,000 vs 4,500). HSC weights rescaled by 1.3 to offset higher fluency. Authors call it initial and ask for replication.
agent_relevance: Suggests the difference lies in weak bridging links between categories, not in the strong links. A scaffold should look for cross-category bridges, not remote single words.

source: Ovando-Tellez, Kenett, Benedek et al. (2022) Brain connectivity-based prediction of real-life creativity is mediated by semantic memory structure (Science Advances)
finding: Independent sample with per-person networks from relatedness judgments. Less modular semantic networks go with more real-life creative activity and achievement. The sign matches 2014 for modularity and path length, but effects are modest.
numbers: 101 healthy adults (48 women, age 22-40). 35 words, 595 pair ratings per person, 0-100 scale; weighted (WUN) and unweighted (UUN, ratings above 50) networks. Spearman: C-Act with WUN ASPL -0.276 (p=.007) and UUN Q -0.281; C-Ach with WUN Q -0.295 (p=.004) and UUN Q predicted. WUN CC with C-Ach .201 (p=.052), not significant. Results held after controlling age, sex, education, IQ. Mediation: brain efficiency to UUN Q beta .305 and Q to C-Ach beta .241; indirect effect .073, 95% CI .018 to .140; total and direct effect not significant (.142, p=.056).
limits: Real-life creativity questionnaire, not lab tasks. Only 35 nodes. Leave-one-out prediction with a permutation test. Clustering and small-worldness were weak or null. Correlational.
agent_relevance: The cleanest individual-level replication. Modularity and path length are the reliable measures, clustering is not. Gives a rough size: rho about 0.2 to 0.3.

source: Skurnik and Kenett (2026) Semantic memory structure and self-evaluation of creativity: evidence across tasks and dimensions
finding: Large new sample, per-person networks. Network integration links weakly to originality and to how original people think their ideas are. Usefulness is mostly unrelated to network structure. Self-ratings diverge from objective ratings.
numbers: Study 1 N=236, creative problem solving task. Ideation fluency with objective originality r=.15 (p=.02); eigenvector centrality with objective originality r=.14 (p=.019); global efficiency with subjective originality r=.14, modularity r=-.14. Objective originality regression F(2,233)=2.83, p=.06, adj R2=.015; fluency beta .03 (p=.019). Usefulness model adj R2=.035, global efficiency beta -.006 (p=.006), modularity beta -.51 (p=.009). Objective vs subjective originality r=.07 (ns). Study 2 within-subject replicates with AUT and CPS.
limits: Effects tiny (adj R2 0.013 to 0.035). Originality model did not reach p<.05 overall. Usefulness has the sign reversed for global efficiency. Network built from a relatedness-judgment task.
agent_relevance: Best sign that the structure effect is small and shifts with task and with originality versus usefulness. Do not rely on network distance for appropriate answers; add a code check for fit.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) Automating creativity assessment with SemDis (Behavior Research Methods)
finding: Semantic distance from word-embedding models (GloVe, CBOW, LSA-type) predicts human creativity ratings strongly. A latent factor over five models works best. It also reproduces the serial-order effect (later ideas are more remote). This is the standard computational proxy for associative distance.
numbers: Five studies. Serial-order study: N=133 adults. Study 4: samples of N=62 and N=56. Correlation with creativity ratings highest for GloVe r=.61 and cbowukwac r=.55; multiplicative composition models correlate .66 to .78 with creativity in Sample 2. Creative-metaphor factor with AUT creativity r=.49 and with AUT semantic distance r=.41.
limits: Distance tracks novelty, and is negatively related to appropriateness (r about -.55 to -.9 in Study 4 Sample 2 tables). A cited study found 'be creative' gives moderate distance, not maximal. Depends on corpus and model.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-computable seed-distance score for O7. Choose a middle distance, not the maximum, because maximal distance becomes nonsense.

source: Luchini, Kaufman, Goecke, Wilhelm, Kenett, Lei, Benedek, van Hell and Beaty (2025) Creativity supports learning through associative thinking (npj Science of Learning)
finding: Students who produce more semantically distant word associations learn more foreign words, even after controlling intelligence. Study 2 extends it to story writing and sketching, with associative thinking as mediator.
numbers: Study 1 about 142 students. Semantic distance (SemDis) of verb-generation responses correlated r=0.33 with day-1 learning and r=0.38 with learning 24 h later. Day 1 recall M=19.64 (SD 11.23), day 2 M=16.34 (SD 10.21), t(141)=7.51, d=0.31.
limits: Undergraduates, one learning test (Lithuanian-English pairs). Correlational, with mediation in Study 2.
agent_relevance: Remote association may help memory writing and retrieval, not only novelty. Weak support for letting the agent store remote links it generated.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) Probing the creativity of large language models: can models produce divergent semantic association?
finding: LLMs were tested on the Divergent Association Task (DAT, distance between 10 unrelated nouns). With greedy decoding GPT-4 beat 96.1% of humans and GPT-3.5-turbo beat the human average. Higher temperature raised scores for other models but not GPT-4, and made output unstable.
numbers: GPT-4 DAT 89.1 (above 96.1% of humans), GPT-3.5-turbo 80.8 (above average human). Temperature varied 0.1 to 1. A naive random sampler of WordNet nouns also beat most humans and models. Without the DAT prompt, models give more related words than the 'random' instruction does.
limits: DAT rewards novelty only and word frequency confounds distance. Humans and models differ in how they pick. Little-c creativity only. Newer GPT-4 versions are in later work.
agent_relevance: Shows an LLM can produce distant words when told to, so distance can be controlled by the prompt rather than by temperature. The random baseline shows distance alone is not creativity (G3 style: need a check on fit).

source: Bellemare-Pepin, Lespinasse, Tholke, Harel, Mathewson, Olson, Bengio and Jerbi (2024) Divergent creativity in humans and large language models
finding: Compared many LLMs with 100,000 humans on the DAT, plus haiku, synopses and flash fiction. GPT-4 beat the human mean; Gemini Pro matched it. The top LLMs stay below highly creative people. Models repeat the same words and newer versions did not always do better.
numbers: Human sample N=100,000; each LLM bar is the mean of 500 responses. GPT-4 above human mean (significant). GPT-4-turbo scored lower than GPT-4; 'ocean' appears in over 90% of GPT-4-turbo word sets; 'microscope' in 70% and 'elephant' in 60% of GPT-4 / GPT-3.5 responses; humans' top words were car 1.4%, dog 1.2%, tree 1.0%. GPT-4 at highest temperature averaged 85.6, above 72% of humans. Strategy prompts (opposition, thesaurus, etymology) changed scores; etymology beat the plain prompt for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
limits: DAT is single-word and novelty-only. Limited outputs are very repetitive, so per-model diversity is low.
agent_relevance: Concrete: a strategy instruction (vary etymology, use a thesaurus) changes the distance of seeds, so O7 can vary seed distance by an instruction. Models need an anti-repeat code check.

source: Anonymous authors (2025) Deep Associations, High Creativity: PACE, parallel association chain evaluation
finding: A benchmark that measures how far an LLM travels in association chains. Scores correlate with model rankings on creative writing. Top models match general human adults, and professionals score higher.
numbers: 110 seed words, 3 associates, then 20-word chains, FastText cosine distance, about 6,270 words per model, 34 models. Spearman with Arena Creative Writing 0.739 (30 models), Arena overall 0.660, LiveBench 0.691 (19), EQ-Bench 0.637 (18), MMLU-Pro 0.505 (23). Embedding matters: GloVe 0.529, MUSE 0.757, FastText 0.739. Human data (Gray et al. 2019, six seeds): high LLMs vs general adults Welch t=0.644, p=0.52; professionals higher, overall t=6.152. Best human 0.8501 vs best model 0.8251; lowest human 0.3457 vs lowest model 0.6888. LLMs have lower type-token ratio.
limits: English only. Small numbers of models for some benchmarks. Human comparison on only six seeds. Authors' identity not recorded here. Chain turns are generated in order, unlike human thought.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to measure chain distance in the agent's own open mode: score each step by distance from all earlier words, then stop on flat distance.

source: Nakajima, Zuiderveld and Pezzelle (2026) Beyond divergent creativity: a human-based evaluation of creativity in LLMs (Findings of EACL 2026)
finding: Abstract only. DAT ignores whether words fit the context. Several top LLMs score below two baselines with no creative ability on DAT. A conditional version (CDAT) scores novelty given appropriateness. Under CDAT smaller model families look most creative and advanced ones favour appropriateness over novelty.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Full text not read, only the abstract page.
agent_relevance: Same warning as Chen and Ding: distance alone is gamed. Pair seed distance with a fit check.

source: Vintar and Javorsek (2025) The truth is no diaper: human and AI-generated associations to emotional words (ICCC'25)
finding: Abstract only. LLM associations to emotional cue words overlap only moderately with human ones, intensify the cue's emotion, and are more predictable and less creative than human ones.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Six-page short paper, full text not read.
agent_relevance: LLM associations lean toward the most probable associate, a steep hierarchy in Mednick's terms. Remote seeds need to be forced.

source: Beaty, Kenett, Hass and Schacter (2023) Semantic memory and creativity: the costs and benefits of semantic memory structure in generating original ideas (Thinking and Reasoning)
finding: Review located by Europe PMC search. Full text could not be fetched (PMC bot check and Europe PMC error).
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. Needed for Angle B.
agent_relevance: Next-step reading for the cost side of a flexible network.

source: Gray, Anderson, Chen, Kelly, Christian, Patrick, Huang, Zhou and Lewis (2019) Forward flow: a new measure to quantify free thought and predict creativity
finding: Located by search only. Forward flow measures how far each free-association word is from all earlier words in the chain. The PACE paper reuses its human data. Rossiter (2020) wrote a critical comment and Kenett et al. replied.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The measure of cumulative distance from all earlier thoughts is directly usable in code for the agent's chains.

source: Kenett and Faust (2019) A semantic network cartography of the creative mind (Trends in Cognitive Sciences)
finding: Located by Europe PMC listing only (115 citations). Review of the network approach to creativity.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Central review for Angle B.

source: Kenett, Anaki and Faust (2014) Mednick-theory framing as stated in the paper
finding: The authors restate Mednick's claim as flat (many, broad) versus steep (few, common) hierarchies, describe the RAT (e.g. Cottage, Swiss, Cake gives Cheese), and link memory search to a search-engine type algorithm. They argue the earlier theory needs a structural test, which they supply with network science.
numbers: RAT in the study: 7 (SD 2.7) in LSC vs 13.2 (SD 3) in HSC, p<0.001. TACT fluency 65.9 vs 88; TACT quality 34 vs 50.4. Novel-metaphor RT 1245 ms vs 874 ms.
limits: RAT is both a selection variable and the outcome in the decision tree, so group contrasts on RAT are partly circular.
agent_relevance: Group selection used RAT scores as the outcome, so the 'creative' label is partly a RAT label. Note this when borrowing the result.

source: Ovando-Tellez et al. (2022) design details: networks from judgments
finding: Per-person weighted and unweighted undirected networks are built from pair relatedness ratings on a small fixed word set. Metrics: ASPL, CC, Q, S. This is the replacement for the 2014 group-network approach.
limits: Only 35 words. Small-worldness near 1 in weighted networks.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, the same relatedness-judgment task could be run on a model to get its network, a test not yet done in anything I opened.

source: Skurnik and Kenett (2026) network metric intercorrelations
finding: Network metrics from one person are highly redundant: global efficiency, clustering, modularity, centrality and degree all move together. So 'shorter paths' and 'lower modularity' are largely one dimension.
numbers: N=236. Global efficiency with CC r=.78; with modularity r=-.75; modularity with eigenvector centrality r=-.85 and with weighted degree r=-.83. Means: CC 0.16 (SD 0.14), global efficiency 29.94 (SD 15.93), Q 0.28 (SD 0.18).
limits: Single task and sample.
agent_relevance: One scalar (integration) is enough for any tracking in the schema; avoid many correlated metrics.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) SemDis: instruction effect on semantic distance
finding: Cited work shows semantic distance depends on instruction: lowest for 'common', highest for 'random', in between for 'creative'. People asked to be creative give novel but still appropriate answers, not maximal distance.
numbers: Three instruction conditions (common < creative < random in distance). Study 3 serial-order data N=133 adults, mean age 19.6, 69% female.
limits: Description of an earlier study as relayed in the paper, not the original numbers.
agent_relevance: Target distance for open mode is 'creative', which is between common and random. Parameter that code can set.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) decoding results
finding: Top-p sampling raised DAT for most models but with unstable and invalid answers. GPT-4 did not gain, because its high-probability tokens were already good answers. Surprisal and DAT are linked for humans and baselines.
numbers: Top-p 0.9 with temperature 0.7 used for sampled runs; temperature range 0.1 to 1. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-turbo exceed the human average at equal surprisal; other models fall short. Oasst-Llama-30B beat Vicuna-13B, which may be explained by rarer words.
limits: Sampling benefit is model dependent.
agent_relevance: Randomness is a poor lever for distance in strong models. Use instruction-controlled seeds and code checks instead.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024) prompt controls
finding: With DAT instructions every model beat a control condition without them. Opposition-meaning strategy lowered scores because opposites (light, darkness) are close in embedding space.
numbers: Contrasts significant except Thesaurus vs Basic for GPT-3.5; Thesaurus beat DAT for GPT-4. Lower-scoring models vary more and often fail to follow instructions.
limits: Embedding distance treats antonyms as near, a measurement artifact.
agent_relevance: Antonym seeds look 'distant' to humans but near to an embedding. Use more than one distance measure.

source: Luchini et al. (2025) goal-directed versus free association
finding: The paper separates goal-directed association (produce a novel but meaningful link, verb generation task) from free association (first word that comes to mind), and finds the effect holds for the goal-directed kind.
numbers: Study 1 r=0.33 (day 1) and 0.38 (day 2). Fluid and crystallised intelligence tests were controlled.
limits: Verb generation, not free association networks.
agent_relevance: Open mode should be goal-directed (novel and fitting), not blind free association.

source: Kenett, Levy, Kenett and Stanley (2018) PNAS limitations and open questions
finding: The authors admit the result needs replication: small group size, 96 cues, free-association networks criticised as a basis for semantic networks, and a smoothing step in the method.
numbers: 33 per group; 3,676 interlinks and 348 intralinks; 8 matched components.
limits: Same data as the 2014 paper.
agent_relevance: Our row's 'replication needed' is correct. Ovando-Tellez 2022 and Skurnik 2026 are the independent confirmations, with small effects.

source: Moonlight review of 'Are semantic networks associated with idea originality in artificial creativity? A comparison with human agents' (secondary summary found in search)
finding: Search snippet only: a semantic network built from ChatGPT-4o outputs was more rigid and segregated than the network of low-creative humans, yet the model gave more original ideas. This would break the human link between network flexibility and originality. Not verified; the page returned HTTP 429.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Secondary aggregator, not opened. Find the original paper before use.
agent_relevance: If true, an LLM's structure does not predict its originality, so structure metrics should not be used to steer the agent.

source: Scientific Reports 2025 (article s41598-025-25157-3) benchmark of LLMs against 100,000 humans on the DAT
finding: Search snippet only: benchmarks several LLMs against a large human cohort with the same scoring and tests prompting and temperature. Page redirected to a login wall.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not opened; may be the journal version of Bellemare-Pepin et al. (a11), unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: Do not count as separate evidence until checked.
